references.text: The synagogue ruler quotes directly from the fourth commandment: 'Six days you shall labor and do all your work' (Exod 20:9–10). He uses the law of the six working days as an argument against Jesus healing on the Sabbath.

The parallel to the Sabbath command in Deuteronomy: 'Six days you shall labor and do all your work. But the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God' (Deut 5:13–14). The synagogue ruler appeals to this Sabbath regulation.
Earlier too, the scribes and Pharisees watched Jesus closely to see if he would heal on the Sabbath, so they could find grounds to accuse him (Luke 6:7).
A similar situation where Jesus asks the lawyers and Pharisees whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath (Luke 14:3), showing the ongoing conflict over Sabbath healings.
In Matthew, the opponents ask the question directly: 'Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?' (Matt 12:10) – the same kind of objection that the synagogue ruler raises here.
In Mark, they kept watch on Jesus to see if he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they could accuse him (Mark 3:2), a pattern repeated in Luke 13:14.

Some of the Pharisees said, 'This man is not from God, for he does not keep the Sabbath' (John 9:16). The same kind of accusation about breaking the Sabbath through healing that the synagogue ruler levels against Jesus.
The Jews persecuted Jesus because he did such things on the Sabbath (John 5:16). The Sabbath conflict was a recurring source of strife between Jesus and the religious leaders.
Jesus' reply to the synagogue ruler follows immediately, where he exposes the hypocrisy in their objection (Luke 13:15–17).
Jesus uses a similar argument in Matthew: If someone rescues a sheep that has fallen into a pit on the Sabbath, how much more is a person worth? (Matt 12:11–12).
